[[File:Marolois, Samuel – Opera mathematica, 1633 – BEIC 195898.jpg|thumb|right|upright|Title page of Marolois' ''Opera mathematica'', 1633]]
'''Samuel Marolois''' ({{ca|1572}} – before 1627) was a Dutch mathematician and military engineer who is best known for his work on [[Perspective (graphical)|perspective]].

== Life and work ==
Marolois (or Marlois) was born {{ca|1572}} in the [[Dutch Republic]] (possibly in [[The Hague]]) as son of Nicolas Marolois, a Protestant native of [[Valenciennes]] who had been exiled from France and served the [[Prince of Orange]].{{sfn|de Waard|1912}}{{sfn|Goudeau|2015}}{{sfn|Andersen|2008|p=297}}
Marolois became a mathematician and earthworks engineer in the employ of [[Maurice, Prince of Orange]]{{sfn|Goudeau|2015}}{{sfn|Andersen|2008|p=297}} He was married to Hester le Maire, which made him a brother-in-law of the Amsterdam merchants Thomas le Maire and Pieter le Fevre. In March 1611, he bought a house in The Hague.{{sfn|de Waard|1912}} After the death of [[Ludolph van Ceulen]], Marolois attempted unsuccessfully to succeed him as Chair of Mathematics in Leiden.{{sfn|de Waard|1912}}{{sfn|Goudeau|2015}}

Marolois wrote a book on [[Perspective (graphical)|perspective]], {{lang|fr|La perspective contenant la theorie et la practique d'icelle}}, which was published in 1614 and printed many times in other languages including Dutch, German and Latin.{{sfn|Andersen|2008|p=297}} The book had both theoretical and practical elements.{{sfn|Andersen|2008|p=298}} The theoretical parts were mostly taken from the works of [[Guidobaldo del Monte]], while the practical parts included many examples. In total, 275 figures are printed in the book.{{sfn|Andersen|2008|p=299}} While Marolois' work contributed little to the mathematical theory of perspective, his book was influential in spreading awareness of the ideas. The artist [[Joshua Kirby]] later claimed it was one of the most important early books on perspective.{{sfn|Andersen|2008|p=309}}

Marolois was a military adviser to the Dutch Republic 1612–1619. His {{lang|fr|Fortification ou architecture militaire}} described the cheapest way to build fortifications.{{sfn|Parker|1976|p=60}} It was the first systematic treatment of the Dutch system of fortifications, using geometric operations to draw polygonal plans, and is famous for the drawing of the citadel of [[Coevorden]].{{sfn|Goudeau|2015}}

Marolois died in The Hague before 1627.{{sfn|de Waard|1912}}{{sfn|Goudeau|2015}} [[Albert Girard]] prepared an edition of his mathematical works that was published in 1628.{{sfn|Field|Gray|1987|p=25}}
